extracted.intended_audience: Brazilian policymakers, IP lawyers, government health and trade officials, and stakeholders evaluating TRIPS compliance of patent law reform
extracted.subtask_description: A legal-technical evaluation of proposed amendments to Brazil's Patent Act (Bill H.R. 5402/2013), assessing whether specific measures (term limits, patentability exclusions, opposition procedures, data protection, ANVISA involvement, government use) are consistent with the TRIPS Agreement and international practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent term limited to 20 years (no extensions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 2 of Bill No. H.R. 5402/2013 revokes Article 40 and limits patent term to 20 years from filing; Article 33 TRIPS requires protection not end before 20 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TRIPS does not require patent-term extensions to compensate for regulatory or grant delays; the 20-year term was adopted partly to compensate for customary regulatory delay. Practical considerations noted: applicants have expectations of eventual grant and may seek retroactive damages; delays should be addressed by INPI capacity improvements; TRIPS Article 62.2 does require reasonable timeliness in rendering patent decisions to avoid unwarranted curtailment of protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude new uses and new forms of known substances from patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Bill Art.10 X and XI: 'any new property or new use of a known substance...unless this known process results in a new product' and 'new forms of known substances that do not result in an improvement in the known efficacy of the substance' are not considered inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to prevent evergreening (granting new 20-year monopolies for minor changes or easily discovered new uses). Mirrors India section 3(d). 'Efficacy' standard suggests patents only where there is significant or dramatic improvement in therapeutic efficacy. New uses often lack novelty/inventive step because they are routine/obvious investigations; TRIPS Article 27.3(a) allows exclusion of diagnostic/therapeutic methods, supporting exclusion of new therapeutic uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'same substance' for derivatives and forms
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of Art.10, 'salts, esters, ethers, polymorphs, metabolites, pure form, size of particles, isomers, mixtures of isomers, complexes, combinations and other derivatives of a known substance shall be considered the same substance, unless they significantly differ in terms of properties regarding efficacy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lists common pharmaceutical variations that will be treated as the same substance unless there is a significant efficacy difference—aimed at excluding routine optimizations (stability, solubility) from new patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: TRIPS minimum patentability standards (novelty, inventive step, industrial application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article 27.1: patents shall be available for inventions provided that they are new, involve an inventive step and are capable of industrial application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TRIPS terms are not exhaustively defined, giving Members interpretive freedom (Article 1.1) to adopt looser or stricter standards according to national needs, subject to minimum treaty requirements. Jurisdictions vary in how strictly they apply these standards (examples cited: Myriad, KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Heightened inventive_step requirement (significant technical advance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed Art.13: 'The invention carries inventive activity when, for a person skilled in the art, it does not derive in an obvious or evident manner from the state of the art, and provided it represents a significant technical advance in regards to the state of the art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brazil may legitimately adopt a heightened inventive-step standard to avoid granting monopolies for minor advances. International precedent supports tighter obviousness analysis (e.g., KSR). This is consistent with TRIPS interpretive flexibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to exclude therapeutic/diagnostic/surgical methods and therapeutic uses
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPS Article 27.3(a) allows Members to exclude 'diagnostic, therapeutic and surgical methods for the treatment of humans' and the Report interprets new therapeutic uses as eligible for such exclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports excluding new uses/methods of use from patentability as they may be considered therapeutic methods or lacking inventive step/novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt pre-grant and post-grant opposition procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed Art.31 allows any interested party to file an opposition from publication until end of exam; applicant notified and may respond within 60 days; examiner may commission technical opinions and must respond to each filed opposition explaining acceptance or rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TRIPS does not prohibit opposition procedures; Article 62.4 references principles governing administrative inter partes procedures. The proposed design (pre-grant opposition, 60-day response, expert technical opinions, mandatory reasoned responses) is reasonable and desirable to improve patent quality and deter unmeritorious applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic submissions of prior art/evidence (intuitive channel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed Art.31-A requires the Patent Office to offer an intuitive, easy-access electronic channel for any person to present evidence or proof of prior existence of the related invention or state of the art, free of charge, and allows submissions even after grant, especially during opposition/post-grant opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitates public participation in examination and opposition; supports improved examination quality and post-grant challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data protection limited to protection against unfair commercial use, not exclusivity
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPS Article 39.3 requires protection of undisclosed test data against unfair commercial use and disclosure where origination involves considerable effort; it does not mandate data exclusivity. Bill clarifies government use of undisclosed data for market approval of equivalent products (§3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brazil's clarification aligns with state practice and expert opinion that data protection need not mean monopolistic data exclusivity. Courts misinterpreting criminal provision as requiring exclusivity should be corrected by statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: ANVISA prior consent and public-health review for pharmaceutical patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed Art.229-C: granting of patents for pharmaceutical products/processes shall depend on prior consent from ANVISA, which shall examine the application in light of public health; ANVISA may deem an application contrary to public health if it presents a health risk or is of interest to access-to-medicines policy and does not meet patentability/other criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although this sets a different review path for pharmaceuticals, TRIPS Article 27's ban on discrimination by field of technology permits differentiation with reasonable justification. Reliance on ANVISA's expertise and documentation of justification should defend against TRIPS challenges; the provision is presented as a focused selection for careful review, not a different substantive patentability standard beyond usual requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government (public, non-commercial) use of patents and patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed Art.43-A: the Government may use patent subject matter or patent applications for non-commercial public interest purposes without consent, directly or via third parties; includes process-product relation, notification of holder, non-exclusivity, and prohibition on sub-licensing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article 31 TRIPS permits involuntary use for public, non-commercial purposes provided notification and adequate remuneration. Brazil's proposal adds permissible features: government-set remuneration guidance, pre-grant government use conditioned on legal deposit of remuneration, and limits on judicial intervention (judiciary shall not decide whether public interest applies and cannot enjoin use during remuneration appeal). These are presented as TRIPS-compliant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remuneration rules for public non-commercial/government use
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed §4–§5 of Art.43-A: remuneration set by Government considering circumstances, customary voluntary-license percentage applied over Government's cost from use, weighed by collaboration by patent holder in technology transfer; for patent applications remuneration legally deposited until grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules aim to satisfy TRIPS requirement of 'adequate remuneration' while allowing government discretion in calculation and permitting pre-grant government use with deposit pending grant. Judiciary limitations on reviewing public-interest determinations and on interrupting government use during appeals are also included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative and judicial limits on government use remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed provisions prevent judiciary from deciding whether public interest purposes apply (§6) and disallow lifting, limiting or interrupting public non-commercial uses by legal appeal over remuneration (§7).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to ensure continuity of government non-commercial uses and align with TRIPS which does not require prior negotiations and allows Member-determined procedures; raises separation-of-powers and due-process considerations but presented as TRIPS-compliant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation of applicants and remedies during pendency (retroactive damages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants in Brazil have an expectation of eventual grant and a right to seek retroactive damages from persons who infringe a pending patent once it is granted, giving de facto exclusive rights during delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical reality is used to argue TRIPS does not mandate patent term extensions as compensation for delays; however, timeliness obligations remain and capacity/backlog reduction is desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: TRIPS interpretive flexibility and public-health priority (Doha Declaration)
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPS Articles 1.1, 75, 86 and the Doha Declaration confirm Members' freedom to implement TRIPS consistent with promoting public health and preventing abuse of IPRs; Members may adopt measures necessary to protect public health and nutrition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as legal basis for Brazil to prioritize access to medicines and to design patentability/examination procedures (e.g., ANVISA involvement, exclusions, government use) that support public health objectives while remaining within TRIPS bounds, provided measures are documented and reasonably justified.
